part_title: EC2 for GenAI: Instance Selection, Bootstrap and Linux Launch Walkthrough

scenes.title: Amazon EC2 for GenAI workloads
scenes.narration: This architecture follows a GenAI application hosted on an EC2 instance. Start with the instance type: inference may need CPU, substantial memory, or a compatible accelerator depending on the model. The bootstrap stage uses user data to install drivers, libraries, and the application, while an attached IAM role provides temporary credentials for S3 or other approved AWS calls. A security group controls inbound and outbound traffic. The user reaches the web UI or API over an allowed connection, and the model runtime processes requests using the installed dependencies. The persistent EBS volume stores approved model artifacts, application files, and logs as appropriate. Pay attention to the different security boundaries. A security group permitting HTTPS is not a substitute for authenticating callers. An IAM role grants AWS API access, not Linux administration. User data is a setup mechanism, not a secrets vault. EC2 offers flexibility for custom inference frameworks and unusual hardware, but you own operating-system patching, instance health, capacity planning, and much of the deployment lifecycle.

scenes.title: EC2 sizing and configuration for inference
scenes.narration: This slide is a sizing decision across six dimensions. Choose an instance family based on whether the work is general purpose, CPU intensive, memory intensive, or accelerated. Estimate the memory needed for model weights, runtime, activations, and concurrent requests; model parameter count alone is not a sufficient sizing calculation. Assess accelerator compatibility: NVIDIA GPU instances suit many frameworks, while Inferentia or other specialized silicon depends on supported runtimes and model compilation. Select EBS capacity and performance for model downloads, caches, and logs; encrypted gp3 or an appropriate higher-performance volume may be needed. Then examine networking bandwidth and placement, especially when large artifacts are loaded over the network. Finally choose a purchase option. On-Demand provides flexibility, commitments help sustained use, and Spot can be cost effective for interruption-tolerant processing but introduces interruption risk. The lower selection path asks you to start from model size, latency objective, throughput, storage, and expected concurrency. Benchmark a representative workload before buying a larger instance, since throughput, time to first token, and memory exhaustion reveal different bottlenecks.

scenes.title: EC2 User Data
scenes.narration: Follow the five-step launch sequence along the top. First include a user-data script while launching the instance. On a supported Linux AMI, cloud-init processes it during the initial boot. The script installs a runtime, places application dependencies, creates a systemd unit, and enables the application service. The final step queries a health endpoint to verify the application actually started. Look at the example commands: package installation is separated from the service definition and the systemctl enable operation. A script returning zero isn't enough if the application process immediately crashes or cannot reach its dependencies. Inspect cloud-init logs, the systemd journal, service status, and the health endpoint when bootstrap fails. One nuance is that many user-data scripts run once by default, so replacing the script is not automatically a rolling update strategy. Use a proper image pipeline, configuration management, or deployment mechanism for repeatable production changes. Never put long-lived passwords or API keys into user data because it may remain accessible to authorized instance administrators.

scenes.title: Launch a Linux EC2 instance
scenes.narration: This console walkthrough moves from the AMI selection to a successful SSH login. Choose the intended Linux image and verify its architecture matches the instance type. Select a cost-appropriate instance size, then configure a key pair and store the private key securely. Next choose the VPC, subnet, and public IP settings. The illustrated lab permits SSH port twenty-two only from the learner's current IP address, avoiding a broad zero-dot-zero-dot-zero-dot-zero slash zero rule. Configure an EBS root volume, review the summary, and launch the instance. After it enters the running state, wait for the instance status checks to pass. The terminal example tightens key-file permissions with chmod four hundred and connects with ssh using the appropriate default user for the selected AMI, such as ubuntu for Ubuntu images. For production, prefer Session Manager where appropriate, private subnets, and carefully controlled administration. A successful SSH prompt proves connectivity to the instance, not that a GenAI model is installed or secured; those are subsequent configuration and validation steps.
